title: Signaling to the Nucleus: CREB, AP-1 and Immediate Early Genes

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: A {{c1::transcription factor}} is a protein that binds a short, specific DNA sequence near a gene and changes how often that gene is copied into RNA.
cards.quote: A transcription factor is a protein that binds a short, specific DNA sequence near a gene and changes how often that gene is copied into RNA.
cards.section: Four ways a signal flips a waiting factor

cards.front: Why do fast signaling pathways modify pre-made transcription factors instead of synthesizing new factors from scratch?
cards.back: Transcription plus translation is slow; making the factor in advance lets the signal simply flip a switch within minutes.
cards.quote: Making more factor from scratch works, but transcription plus translation is slow. Fast pathways modify a pre-made factor in one of four ways:
cards.section: Four ways a signal flips a waiting factor

cards.front: What are the four ways a fast signaling pathway switches on a pre-made transcription factor, with one example of each?
cards.back: Add a phosphate to bind a co-activator (CREB); remove phosphates for nuclear entry (NFAT); destroy an inhibitor (NF-κB/IκB); make the messenger the factor (STATs, Smads, or cleaved Notch).
cards.quote: In all four, synthesis is done in advance, so the signal only flips the switch.
cards.section: Four ways a signal flips a waiting factor

cards.front: A {{c1::co-activator}} does not bind DNA itself, but is brought to a gene by a transcription factor that does.
cards.quote: A co-activator does not bind DNA itself but is brought to a gene by a factor that does.
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: CREB sits largely on DNA as a pair bound to the eight-letter {{c1::cAMP response element (CRE)}}, TGACGTCA, before any signal arrives.
cards.quote: CREB (cAMP response element-binding protein) binds the eight-letter cAMP response element (CRE), TGACGTCA, as a pair and sits largely on DNA before any signal arrives.
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: In the cAMP–PKA–CREB pathway, why does CREB sitting on DNA leave the gene off until cAMP rises, and how does cAMP turn it on?
cards.back: DNA occupancy alone leaves the gene off; cAMP frees PKA catalytic subunits that enter the nucleus and phosphorylate CREB on serine 133, letting CREB hold a co-activator.
cards.quote: Occupancy alone leaves the gene off. Picking up from the cAMP and PKA lesson, cAMP frees PKA catalytic subunits, and some enter the nucleus to phosphorylate serine 133.
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: Once recruited to phosphorylated CREB, by what two mechanisms does the co-activator CBP promote transcription?
cards.back: CBP acetylates nearby histones, loosening packaged DNA, and contacts the RNA polymerase machinery.
cards.why: CBP's KIX domain grips CREB far more tightly once serine 133 is phosphorylated.
cards.quote: grips CREB far more tightly once serine 133 is phosphorylated, then acetylates nearby histones (loosening packaged DNA) and contacts the RNA polymerase machinery.
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: Besides cAMP/PKA, which two signaling routes converge on CREB serine 133?
cards.back: Calcium–calmodulin activates nuclear CaMKIV (helped by CaMKK), and growth factors act through ERK-activated kinases—not ERK directly—to phosphorylate the same serine 133.
cards.quote: From the calcium lesson, calcium–calmodulin activates nuclear CaMKIV, which hits the exact same serine 133; growth factors also reach it via ERK-activated kinases (not ERK directly).
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: A cell makes only a mutant CREB in which serine 133 is changed to alanine, while PKA and CaMKIV are normal. What happens to CREB's DNA occupancy and CBP binding after cAMP or calcium rises, and why?
cards.back: CREB still sits largely on its CRE site, but tight CBP binding fails after both cAMP and calcium rises. Both PKA and CaMKIV must phosphorylate serine 133 so CBP's KIX domain can grip CREB tightly, and alanine cannot be phosphorylated.
cards.quote: The KIX domain of CBP (CREB-binding protein) grips CREB far more tightly once serine 133 is phosphorylated,
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: A neuron receives glutamate while its membrane is held hyperpolarized so it cannot depolarize. What happens to calcium entry through NMDA receptors and L-type channels and to rapid nuclear CREB phosphorylation, and why?
cards.back: Calcium entry through both channels and rapid CREB phosphorylation fail. Without depolarization, magnesium ions continue blocking glutamate-bound NMDA receptors and L-type voltage-gated calcium channels stay closed, preventing Ca²⁺–calmodulin–CaMKIV activation.
cards.quote: Depolarization opens L-type voltage-gated calcium channels and clears the magnesium ion blocking glutamate-bound NMDA receptors.
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: After strong neuronal firing triggers CaMKIV to phosphorylate CREB serine 133, a nuclear phosphatase immediately strips serine 133 while the slower Ras–ERK kinase route is blocked. What happens to CBP and transcription, and why?
cards.back: CBP detaches and transcription stops. Without sustained phosphorylation of serine 133—normally maintained during strong or prolonged activity by the slower Ras–ERK kinase route—CBP's KIX domain loses its tight grip on CREB.
cards.quote: If a phosphatase strips serine 133 immediately, KIX loses its tight grip, CBP detaches, and transcription stops.
cards.section: CREB: one serine, two messengers

cards.front: How does calcineurin activate NFAT in T cells, and how does this contrast with how PKA activates CREB?
cards.back: Calcineurin strips about a dozen phosphates that hide NFAT's nuclear import signal, letting NFAT enter the nucleus; CREB already sits on DNA and gains one phosphate to bind CBP.
cards.quote: The first film showed NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) flipping in reverse—entering the nucleus when calcineurin strips about a dozen phosphates that hide its nuclear import signal.
cards.section: Calcineurin and NFAT: removing phosphates opens the door

cards.front: After T-cell receptor stimulation sustains store-operated calcium entry and sends NFAT into the nucleus, intracellular calcium drops back to resting levels. What happens to NFAT's phosphorylation state and location, and why?
cards.back: NFAT regains its phosphates and exits the nucleus. When calcium falls, calcineurin is no longer activated by calcium–calmodulin, allowing kinases to restore the phosphates that drive nuclear export.
cards.quote: When calcium drops, kinases restore the phosphates and NFAT exits.
cards.section: Calcineurin and NFAT: removing phosphates opens the door

cards.front: Once inside the T-cell nucleus, NFAT binds DNA beside a Fos–Jun pair on genes such as {{c1::interleukin-2}}, which tells the T cell to divide.
cards.quote: Once inside the nucleus, NFAT binds DNA beside a Fos–Jun pair (met right after the second film) on genes such as interleukin-2, which tells the T cell to divide.
cards.section: Calcineurin and NFAT: removing phosphates opens the door

cards.front: How do the chemically unalike transplant drugs FK506 and cyclosporin A both block calcineurin in T cells?
cards.back: FK506 binds FKBP12 and cyclosporin A binds cyclophilin; each drug–helper complex—not either component alone—sits beside calcineurin's catalytic site and blocks bulky substrates such as NFAT.
cards.quote: Neither drug nor helper blocks calcineurin alone—the pair sits beside the catalytic site and blocks bulky substrates such as NFAT.
cards.section: Calcineurin and NFAT: removing phosphates opens the door

cards.front: A T cell is treated with cyclosporin A and stimulated through its receptor, producing normal store-operated calcium entry. Predict NFAT's phosphorylation state, location, and interleukin-2 transcription, and explain why.
cards.back: NFAT keeps its phosphates, remains in the cytoplasm, and interleukin-2 stays off. Cyclosporin A bound to cyclophilin jams calcineurin despite high calcium, leaving NFAT's nuclear import signal hidden.
cards.quote: Jam calcineurin and NFAT keeps its phosphates and stays in the cytoplasm, so the interleukin-2 gene stays quiet.
cards.section: Calcineurin and NFAT: removing phosphates opens the door

cards.front: Because FKBP12 and cyclophilin are enzymes themselves, test-tube inhibition did not prove calcineurin was the target of FK506 and cyclosporin A in living T cells. What experiment tested this, and what result supported calcineurin as the target?
cards.back: Overproducing calcineurin in T cells made the cells more resistant to both FK506 and cyclosporin A—requiring higher drug doses to silence NFAT—and boosted NFAT-driven transcription.
cards.why: Extra calcineurin leaves more enzyme unbound at any given drug dose; if more enzyme requires more drug, that enzyme is probably the real target.
cards.quote: The cells should become more resistant to both drugs, needing higher doses to silence NFAT, because extra calcineurin leaves more enzyme unbound.
cards.section: Calcineurin and NFAT: removing phosphates opens the door

cards.front: A T cell is engineered to lack FKBP12 while keeping normal levels of cyclophilin and calcineurin. Predict whether FK506 or cyclosporin A can still silence interleukin-2 transcription after receptor stimulation, and why.
cards.back: FK506 loses its effect so interleukin-2 still turns on, whereas cyclosporin A still silences interleukin-2. Neither drug inhibits calcineurin alone: FK506 requires FKBP12 to block calcineurin, while cyclosporin A still forms an inhibitory complex with cyclophilin.
cards.quote: In 1991 Schreiber's group and collaborators showed where they converge: each drug–helper complex binds and inhibits calcineurin.
cards.section: Calcineurin and NFAT: removing phosphates opens the door

cards.front: How can a single transcription factor compute an OR gate that turns a gene on in response to either cAMP or calcium?
cards.back: Keep the factor bound to DNA with one serine phosphorylated by two separate kinases—PKA after cAMP or CaMKIV after calcium—so either messenger recruits the co-activator.
cards.quote: For OR, copy CREB: a DNA-bound factor with one serine hit by two kinases.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Design a single synthetic transcription factor that computes an AND gate—activating transcription only when both calcium and cAMP rise together—and state which signaling rules it rests on.
cards.back: Split nuclear localization and co-activator binding: use calcium/calcineurin dephosphorylation to unmask a nuclear import signal (the NFAT rule) and cAMP/PKA phosphorylation to create the co-activator handle (the CREB rule).
cards.why: Calcium alone imports an inactive factor; cAMP alone phosphorylates a factor trapped in the cytoplasm. Only both messengers together turn the gene on.
cards.quote: For AND, split location and activity. Let calcium/calcineurin unmask a nuclear import signal (as in NFAT), and let cAMP/PKA phosphorylate the co-activator handle.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: CREB, Fos, and Jun are {{c1::bZIP}} (basic leucine zipper) proteins built from two stretches of one long α-helix.
cards.quote: CREB, Fos, and Jun are bZIP (basic leucine zipper) proteins, built from two stretches of one long α-helix:
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: In a bZIP protein, what are the distinct roles of the leucine zipper and the basic stretch, and which residues make the basic stretch bind DNA?
cards.back: The leucine zipper joins two helices via hydrophobic leucines; the basic stretch—rich in positively charged lysine and arginine—parts like chopsticks into the DNA major groove to read a half-site.
cards.quote: rich in positively charged lysine and arginine; beyond the zipper, the helices part like chopsticks so each basic stretch enters the DNA major groove and reads one half-site.
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: An α-helix turns once every ~3.6 residues, and a leucine zipper places a leucine at nearly every 7th residue. How many helical turns span 7 residues, and what geometry does that create?
cards.back: 7 / 3.6 ≈ 1.94 turns—just shy of two full turns—so every seventh residue lands on nearly the same side, forming a gently twisting hydrophobic stripe along the helix.
cards.why: Two helices wind their gently twisting leucine stripes together to hide the hydrophobic leucines from water.
cards.quote: seven residues span 7 / 3.6 ≈ 1.94 turns—just shy of two full turns—so every seventh residue lands on nearly the same side,
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: {{c1::AP-1}} (activator protein 1) is classically a Fos–Jun or Jun–Jun pair, though both can pair with other bZIPs.
cards.quote: AP-1 (activator protein 1) is classically a Fos–Jun or Jun–Jun pair (though both can pair with other bZIPs).
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: Why can Jun pair stably with Jun whereas Fos cannot pair stably with Fos, and how does Fos–Jun DNA binding compare with Jun–Jun?
cards.back: Negatively charged residues flanking Fos's zipper repel each other, preventing Fos–Fos dimers; Fos requires a partner such as Jun, and Fos–Jun grips DNA more tightly than Jun–Jun.
cards.quote: Fos cannot pair stably with Fos because negatively charged residues flanking its zipper repel each other, so Fos needs a partner (classically Jun),
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: How do the preferred DNA binding sites of AP-1 and CREB differ in length and sequence?
cards.back: AP-1 prefers the seven-letter site TGACTCA, one letter shorter than the eight-letter CRE site (TGACGTCA) bound by CREB.
cards.quote: AP-1 prefers the seven-letter site TGACTCA, one letter shorter than the eight-letter CRE (TGACGTCA).
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: If a cell expresses 8 distinct bZIP proteins that can all pair freely with themselves or one another (order does not matter), how many different pairs can form?
cards.back: n(n + 1) / 2 = 8 × 9 / 2 = 36 distinct pairs (8 same-partner pairs plus 8 × 7 / 2 = 28 mixed pairs).
cards.quote: n proteins that can all pair with one another make n(n + 1) / 2 different pairs
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: A cell expresses 5 Fos-family and 4 Jun-family proteins. Jun pairs with any Jun (including itself) or any Fos; Fos never pairs with Fos. How many distinct pairs can form, compared with 9 freely pairing proteins?
cards.back: Under the Fos rule: 4 × 5 / 2 = 10 Jun–Jun pairs + 5 × 4 = 20 Fos–Jun pairs + 0 Fos–Fos = 30 pairs. Nine freely pairing proteins form 9 × 10 / 2 = 45 pairs.
cards.quote: Five freely pairing proteins form 5 × 6 / 2 = 15 pairs. Under the Fos rule: 2 Jun make 2 × 3 / 2 = 3 Jun–Jun pairs,
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: A mutation replaces several positively charged lysine and arginine residues in a bZIP protein's basic stretch with negatively charged residues, leaving its leucine zipper intact. Predict the effects on dimerization and DNA binding, and explain why.
cards.back: The mutant still forms dimers, but the dimer fails to grip DNA properly. By the bZIP two-stretch rule, dimerization depends on the hydrophobic leucine zipper, whereas DNA major-groove binding relies on the positively charged basic stretch.
cards.quote: Basic stretch: rich in positively charged lysine and arginine; beyond the zipper, the helices part like chopsticks so each basic stretch enters the DNA major groove
cards.section: Basic leucine zippers: pairing multiplies DNA choices

cards.front: An {{c1::immediate early gene (IEG)}} is transcribed within minutes of a signal without new protein synthesis.
cards.quote: An immediate early gene (IEG) is transcribed within minutes of a signal without new protein synthesis, defined by the cycloheximide test:
cards.section: Immediate early genes: from minutes to hours

cards.front: How does the cycloheximide test operationally identify an immediate early gene?
cards.back: Block ribosomes with cycloheximide, add the signal, and measure mRNA: an immediate early gene's mRNA still rises within minutes because it uses pre-made transcription factors.
cards.quote: defined by the cycloheximide test: block ribosomes with cycloheximide, add the signal, and measure mRNA.
cards.section: Immediate early genes: from minutes to hours

cards.front: Why can cAMP, calcium, and growth factors all rapidly switch on c-fos transcription via pre-made factors?
cards.back: The c-fos promoter carries both a CRE (bound by CREB) and a serum response element (SRE), bound by SRF and partners such as ERK-phosphorylated Elk-1.
cards.quote: Thus cAMP, calcium, and growth factors all reach c-fos via pre-made factors.
cards.section: Immediate early genes: from minutes to hours

cards.front: Resting fibroblasts receive cycloheximide before growth factor. Predict what happens to c-fos mRNA and Fos protein at 30 minutes, and to an AP-1–driven second-wave mRNA at 2 hours, and explain why.
cards.back: At 30 minutes, c-fos mRNA rises (pre-made factors need no ribosomes), but Fos protein does not rise (stopped ribosomes cannot translate it). At 2 hours, second-wave mRNA stays off because it requires newly made Fos and other first-wave products.
cards.quote: At 30 minutes, c-fos mRNA rises (pre-made factors need no ribosomes), but Fos protein does not rise (stopped ribosomes cannot translate it).
cards.section: Immediate early genes: from minutes to hours

cards.front: How does the two-wave gene program turn a minutes-long extracellular signal into an hours-long cellular response?
cards.back: Pre-made factors rapidly transcribe first-wave genes such as c-fos; newly translated Fos then pairs with Jun to form AP-1, switching on a slower second wave of genes.
cards.quote: Without cycloheximide, newly translated Fos pairs with Jun to form AP-1, switching on a slower second wave of genes that turns a minutes-long signal into an hours-long program.
cards.section: Immediate early genes: from minutes to hours

cards.front: A T cell is pretreated with cycloheximide before T-cell receptor stimulation triggers sustained calcium entry. Does NFAT enter the nucleus, and what would you expect for a composite NFAT plus Fos-Jun target gene like interleukin-2? Name the rules used.
cards.back: NFAT still enters the nucleus: calcium-calcineurin dephosphorylates pre-made NFAT without ribosomes. Interleukin-2 also needs a Fos-Jun partner beside NFAT, and Fos comes from newly translated c-fos, so cycloheximide would be expected to blunt interleukin-2 unless Fos-Jun was already present.
cards.quote: At 2 hours, the second-wave mRNA stays off because it requires newly made Fos and other first-wave products.
cards.section: Immediate early genes: from minutes to hours

cards.front: After a task, brain region A shows no Fos antibody staining while region B stains strongly 2 hours later. Why can you neither conclude region A was silent nor pinpoint the exact second region B fired?
cards.back: A neuron can fire without making Fos, so absent staining does not prove silence; and Fos staining is a snapshot with timing no finer than hours, so it cannot resolve second-by-second activity.
cards.why: Resting neurons make little Fos, and strong excitation induces c-fos via calcium and CREB over hours.
cards.quote: Two cautions apply: a neuron can fire without making Fos, and the stain is a snapshot with timing no finer than hours.
cards.section: Mapping active neurons with Fos

cards.front: What core cellular difference separates brief synaptic strengthening from long-lasting synaptic strengthening?
cards.back: A brief synaptic change modifies existing proteins at the synapse, whereas a long-lasting change requires new transcription, involving CREB where tested.
cards.quote: A brief synaptic change modifies existing proteins; a long-lasting change requires new transcription, involving CREB where tested.
cards.section: From ion channels to CREB and long-term memory

cards.front: In Aplysia sensory neurons, injecting excess short CRE DNA ("decoy CRE DNA") into the nucleus spared short-lasting synaptic strengthening after training but abolished long-lasting strengthening. What mechanism explains this result?
cards.back: Decoy CRE DNA sequesters CREB away from real genes, preventing the new transcription required for long-lasting strengthening, while short-lasting strengthening survives because it modifies proteins already at the synapse.
cards.quote: Short-lasting strengthening survives (it modifies proteins already at the synapse), whereas long-lasting strengthening fails because decoy DNA sequesters CREB.
cards.section: From ion channels to CREB and long-term memory

cards.front: A neuron expresses a blocking form of CREB before repeated training, and synaptic strength is tested immediately and hours later. Predict both outcomes and explain why this does not prove memories are stored in CREB.
cards.back: Short-lasting strengthening survives because it modifies existing synaptic proteins, whereas long-lasting strengthening fails because it requires CREB-driven transcription. Showing CREB is required to trigger long-term change does not show that the memory itself is stored in CREB.
cards.quote: None of this shows that CREB is where a memory is stored.
cards.section: From ion channels to CREB and long-term memory

cards.front: What structural transition occurs in CREB's kinase-inducible domain when phosphorylated CREB binds CBP's KIX domain?
cards.back: CREB's kinase-inducible domain is largely disordered alone and folds into two helices upon binding CBP's KIX domain when serine 133 is phosphorylated.
cards.quote: CREB's kinase-inducible domain is largely disordered alone and folds into two helices upon binding CBP's KIX domain when serine 133 is phosphorylated.
cards.section: CRTC co-activators and coupled folding on CREB

cards.front: For a neuronal CRE target gene that requires both CBP and a CRTC co-activator, predict transcription after cAMP alone versus both cAMP and calcium, and state the rule governing CRTC.
cards.back: cAMP alone is insufficient; both cAMP and calcium are required for full activation. By the CRTC coincidence-detector rule, CRTC enters the nucleus only when calcineurin (calcium) dephosphorylates it and cAMP silences the kinases holding it out.
cards.quote: CRTC co-activators, which enter the nucleus when calcineurin dephosphorylates them and cAMP silences the kinases holding them out—making those genes coincidence detectors for calcium and cAMP.
cards.section: CRTC co-activators and coupled folding on CREB

cards.front: Although 50 human bZIPs could form 1,275 dimers if all paired freely, what structural feature restricts which bZIP helices actually pair stably?
cards.back: Charged residues flanking the hydrophobic leucine stripe set which helices pair stably, as in acidic-residue repulsion blocking Fos–Fos while permitting Fos–Jun.
cards.quote: Charged residues flanking the hydrophobic leucine stripe set which helices pair stably (as in acidic-residue repulsion blocking Fos–Fos while permitting Fos–Jun).
cards.section: bZIP partner specificity across species

cards.front: Why were later mouse CREB memory knockout studies less uniform than the 1994 knockout, and what general experimental caution do they illustrate?
cards.back: The original mutants still made a third CREB isoform, outcomes depended on gene dosage and training spacing, and CREB-deficient mice upregulated the related factor CREM, which may partly stand in—illustrating that residual isoforms, protocol parameters, and paralog compensation can alter knockout phenotypes.
cards.quote: outcomes depended on gene dosage and training spacing, and CREB-deficient mice upregulated the related factor CREM, which may partly stand in for CREB.
cards.section: Why later mouse CREB memory studies varied
